name: mame
why: Emulates thousands of arcade machines and their hardware, a deep door into old chips and firmware.

brief.what_it_is: MAME is a multi-purpose emulation framework, a large open-source program that emulates the hardware of arcade machines and, since it absorbed the sister project MESS, many vintage computers, video game consoles and calculators. The homepage describes it as documenting hardware so that old software stays usable. The pages I read do not spell out exactly what files or inputs you supply, or how the emulated machine's video, sound and controls reach your screen. The homepage's news says it emulates thousands of distinct hardware architectures.
brief.why_it_exists: The stated purpose is to preserve decades of software history before vintage hardware and software are lost. The README says the source code serves as documentation of the hardware, and that running the software is mainly a way to validate that the documentation is accurate.
brief.how_it_works: According to the README, the MAME source code is itself the hardware documentation, and the emulator's usefulness as a working program is secondary to proving the recreation is faithful. The homepage says the project works by documenting hardware and how it functions. The pages I read do not go into the emulation internals, such as CPU cores or timing models.

brief.install_notes: The README points to the docs site (docs.mamedev.org, Compiling MAME page) for prerequisites on macOS and popular Linux distributions. It says recent macOS needs Xcode with command-line tools and SDL 2.0. On Windows, the project provides a MinGW-w64 build environment at mamedev.org/tools, and Visual Studio builds still need that same MinGW-w64 environment. The homepage's 0.286 news notes that SDL3 can be selected for builds with OSD=sdl or OSD=sdl3, and that macOS defaults to SDL3. The homepage also offers prebuilt 64-bit Windows binary packages and says Windows binaries now include SDL sound output and joystick input modules. The brew formula installs an executable named mame. The pages I read cover building from source and do not mention any accounts, licences to accept, or ROM-related first-run steps.
brief.standout: Its stated aim is preservation through documentation: the source code is treated as the spec for the hardware, and running software is the test that the spec is right. The homepage's news shows an active rhythm of monthly releases that add systems such as NS32000-based machines, classic Mac OS on PowerPCs, and A/UX.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists MAME 0.289 dated 31 Jul 2026 as the newest release, preceded by 0.288 on 29 May 2026, 0.287 on 31 Mar 2026, 0.286 on 26 Feb 2026 and 0.285 on 30 Jan 2026. The GitHub README copyright reads 1997-2026. The project also runs CI badges for Linux, Windows and macOS.
brief.caveats: Caution: the homepage has a post dated 01 Apr 2026, 'Future plans announcement', that describes a Rust migration and mandatory AI-assisted code review. The later 07 Apr 2026 post refers to 'our April Fools' Day announcement', so treat the 1 April post as a joke and do not report it as real. The 07 Apr post does describe real upcoming changes: C++20 is required, GCC 11 is the oldest supported version, Windows 10 or later is required, the debugger needs Qt 6, the 32-bit x86 recompiler is being removed, and so are OpenSolaris and System V support, PowerPC-specific optimisations, the macOS aueffectutil tool and the prebuilt MSYS2 environments. The README notes that the Windows toolchain is MinGW-w64, and the macOS path needs Xcode and SDL 2.0. The overall licence is GPL-2.0 or later, with most files under BSD-3-Clause. The name 'MAME' is a registered trademark, so using the name, logo or wordmark needs permission. The pages I read do not explain where software or game data should come from, which is a gap for anyone trying it for the first time.

entry.title: MAME
entry.tldr: An emulator whose source code doubles as documentation for thousands of arcade boards, computers, consoles and calculators, built to preserve old hardware.
entry.deeper_look:
MAME stands for Multiple Arcade Machine Emulator. It began with arcade cabinets and, after absorbing its sister project MESS, now also covers vintage computers, game consoles and calculators. The homepage says it emulates thousands of distinct hardware architectures.

The stated purpose is preservation: "MAME's purpose is to preserve decades of software history." Old hardware fails and the software on it goes with it. The README makes an unusual claim about how that works: "The source code to MAME serves as this documentation." Running software is mainly a way to check that the documentation is accurate. A game that plays correctly is evidence that the written description of the chips and boards is right.

That framing is what makes it a door into something larger. Each supported machine is a worked description of real hardware: its processors, memory maps, video and sound chips. Reading how a machine is described in the source is a way to learn how that machine actually worked.

The project is active, with roughly monthly releases. Recent news mentions additions such as NS32000-based machines, classic Mac OS on PowerPC, and A/UX.
entry.install:
brew install mame

MAME emulates hardware, so the software for a machine (ROMs, disk images) is separate. The pages behind this entry do not say where to get it or how first run works, so check the docs on mamedev.org.

entry.whats_unique: The source code is treated as the specification of the hardware, and running software is the test that the spec is right. Preservation, not play, is the stated goal.
